extracted.intended_audience: patent prosecutors, patent litigators, patent examiners, and patent agents working on U.S. §101 eligibility for software/technical inventions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation criteria for drafting patents and litigating U.S. patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101 (Alice framework), with practice tips drawn from Federal Circuit decisions (Berkheimer, BASCOM, Cardionet, Cellspin, Chamberlain, ChargePoint, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific description of arrangement and component positioning
rubrics_metrics.description: When drafting specifications, consider being specific in description of the arrangement and relative positioning of components of the system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A specifically described arrangement provides a position supporting a technical improvement. In addition, more specific arrangement precludes allegations of pre-emption. (Representative claim context: content filtering system/BASCOM)

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide problem/solution and repeatedly state advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: When drafting your patent application, consider providing 'problem/solution' in the specification to highlight the various inventive concepts of your software related invention as an improvement over known prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider explicitly and repeatedly stating advantages of your inventive concept that support the inventive concept captured in your claims as not routine or conventional. (Berkheimer practice tip #1)

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture inventive concept in dependent claims; do not rely solely on representative independent claim
rubrics_metrics.description: When filing an appeal to a 101 rejection, do not always rely on your independent claim as representative of all the pending claims at issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider identifying each dependent claim that has an additional limitation that is supported in the specification as an inventive concept improvement over known prior art. The Federal Circuit found that dependent claims 4–7 could present factual questions about inventive concept even when the independent claim was found abstract. (Berkheimer practice tip #2)

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice Step 1 — show claims focus on specific means/method that improve technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the claim 'is directed to' an abstract idea (step 1) or instead to a specific means or method that improves a technological process or device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court decisions (e.g., Cardionet) emphasize that claims which 'focus on a specific means or method that improves' a technology are less likely to be characterized as abstract. Provide technical detail in the specification to demonstrate the claimed improvement. Rely on the intrinsic record to understand what the claims are directed to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice Step 2 — conventionality is a question of fact; supply evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Alice step 2, whether a claim element or combination is 'well-understood, routine and conventional' to a skilled artisan is a question of fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factual disputes about whether an aspect of the claims is inventive may preclude dismissal at pleadings or summary judgment (Berkheimer, Aatrix). When there is no genuine issue of material fact the question can be decided as a matter of law, but to avoid adverse rulings supply evidence (intrinsic or extrinsic) showing the inventive concept is not routine or conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize unconventional aspects in specification (do not bury them in abstract-idea context)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the application and claims relate to abstract ideas, any unconventional aspects of the technology should be emphasized and detailed in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid describing the unconventional feature only in the context of the abstract idea; instead describe it as a technical improvement and document how it differs from known systems (BSG Tech practice tip).

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe technical details and technical advantages in the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide technical details in the specification that explain how the invention improves functionality, efficiency, or other technological aspects of devices/systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts find the specification persuasive in determining what claims are directed to (Cardionet). For example, describing how storing objects without redundancy 'improves system operating efficiency and reduces storage costs' supported factual disputes about inventive concept (Berkheimer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use factual dispute examples to resist early dismissal (pleadings/12(b)(6)/summary judgment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Argue the Berkheimer/Aatrix line of cases when there are clear factual disputes about inventive aspects to avoid motions to dismiss or summary judgment under §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include alleging unconventional separation of functions across devices or specific pairing/communication arrangements (Cellspin). Document such factual differences in declaration evidence or specification text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid broad 'need' statements or background framing that characterize the invention as the abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful regarding 'need' statements in the background that could be used to characterize the invention as a broad abstract idea (e.g., 'need for a communication network' leading to 'network-controlled charging stations').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification frames the invention too broadly, courts may treat the claimed invention as an abstract idea. Instead, frame the problem narrowly as a technical problem and tie claimed features to technical solutions (ChargePoint practice tip).

rubrics_metrics.name: New elements that are generic (e.g., wireless transmission) may be treated as abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume that adding a generic technology (like wireless transmission) will supply an inventive concept; courts may view such additions as part of the abstract idea if other claim elements are well-known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful whether the claimed 'new' element is itself abstract or merely a generic implementation of the abstract idea; argue and document how it provides a technical improvement beyond generic use (Chamberlain practice tip).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that merely collect and compare known information risk ineligibility unless a step acts on the comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that perform only 'collecting and comparing known information' have been held ineligible, but claims that perform a step based on the comparison (or include a technical processing/immunization step) can be eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your claim performs any step based on a comparison of collected data or includes a technical action (e.g., immunization step in Classen analog), include and emphasize that in the claim and specification so the claim is not a bare information-collection/comparison abstraction.
